body:
One-on-one time with each daughter taught me something I didn't expect.
They didn't just open up more — they made decisions differently when their sisters weren't watching.
Like they needed that quiet space to figure out who they were on their own.
cta: did you notice this with your kids too?

body:
Write a letter on a big piece of paper, then hide things around the house that start with that sound.
Your kid finds them, names them, drops them in a bowl.
That's the whole game. Loud, silly, and it sticks. 🎯
cta: what sound would you start with?

destination: teaching a life lesson through a story
body:
Pick a short fable and read it together — then ask: what would YOU have done if you were the fox? The crow? The ant?
Kids reveal so much when the lesson belongs to a character, not to them.
Safer to be honest when it's not technically about you. 🦊

body:
Grab a handful of small objects from around the house — a spoon, a sock, a leaf, a coin.
Take turns giving one-word clues until someone guesses the object. That's it. No prep, no rules, just words.
Mine got surprisingly competitive over a wooden spoon. 🙂

body:
My daughter once spent a whole afternoon just tracing letters in spilled flour on the counter.
Not because I asked. Because it felt like drawing, not learning.
That's the part that still stays with me — she had no idea she was practicing.

body:
Rainy afternoon, three girls, nowhere to be.
I didn't plan anything. I just said: figure out what you want to do today.
Watching them negotiate that — without me stepping in — taught me more than any structured activity ever did.

body:
Say a simple word out loud — 'cat,' 'sun,' 'dog' — and ask your kid to draw it before they spell it.
That tiny gap between hearing and drawing is where new words actually land.
Works in any language. Works especially well with English if it's not their first.
cta: tried anything like this with your kids?
